item.content:encoded:
A couple weeks ago we found an email in our inbox from Oakland-based photographer John Coyne. Apparently, he liked the Lumière joint enough to tell us that he was gonna go out and put together some visuals for it. Next thing we know, another email from John arrives over the weekend attached with a cool video he shot using Lumière as the soundtrack.

Just like vocalists take our Riddims to make their own tunes (and just like we snatch sounds from other artists to make tracks of our own!) it’s super dope to see artists from other disciplines taking inspiration from this music and creating their own art with it. After all, such is the culture of the modern Cinemetropolis, no?

Enjoy, and thank John!

item.description: Last month, shortly after Cougfest, the homie Thig Nat from The Physics was gracious enough to open the studio during his lunch break for an afternoon session. While Thig headed back to the day job, Saba and I ran into some technical difficulties and ended up not recording a damn thing. At least some cool [...]
item.content:encoded:
Last month, shortly after Cougfest, the homie Thig Nat from The Physics was gracious enough to open the studio during his lunch break for an afternoon session. While Thig headed back to the day job, Saba and I ran into some technical difficulties and ended up not recording a damn thing.

At least some cool photos came out of the fail, thanks to photographer Greg Nissen and his Leica M2 (50mm Summicron Collapsible, Neopan 400 @ 1600, Ilford DD-X, 13 minutes 68F). In light of our audio engineering impotency, we ended up chopping it up over rangefinders, his hometown of Eugene, Oregon, and Thai Food. Cool dude. Even let a brother borrow his Leica M3 for a test run.

Later, we jetted back to Zia’s spot on Beacon Hill near where we recorded The Long March & Bayani, recording off the same setup we’ve done for years, and banging out three tracks in one night. Felt like old times. Lesson of the day: record where you’re most comfortable and familiar (and then post photos of yourself in a more professional studio to give off the image of #raplife).

More photos after the jump.

item.title: A Few Words On The Teacher Who Played Our Music And Got Put On Leave Last Week
item.dc:creator: bluescholars
item.description: A Few Words On The Teacher Who Played Our Music And Got Put On Leave Last Week
item.content:encoded:
Last Wednesday, we received a couple emails saying that a teacher in Spokane played, and printed the lyrics to, our song “Commencement Day” (The Long March EP, 2005) to his Senior English class on the first day of school. Awesome. The bad news? He got put on administrative leave for it. Aghast, we blasted the news, at the time still unconfirmed by the school or media, on our own and the Blue Scholars Twitter and Facebook accounts, which was followed by a wave of responses online.

After the Spokane School District confirmed the incident, media outlets hit us up to talk about the ordeal. Online comment boards caught on fire. Local nighttime news and classic rock radio host Bob Rivers interviewed us. We ended up declining or missing other interview requests as it got overwhelming.

From an unfortunate situation, it was good to see people getting riled up, whatever shade of opinion, over the issue of education. With all these divisive, manufactured “issues” (i.e. where a mosque should or shouldn’t be built) dominating the airwaves, it was a breath of fresh air to see folks talk about something much closer to home for most of us.

Our primary objective was to make sure that this incident didn’t come and go without at least a few of you knowing about it. At the same time, we wanted to respect the teacher’s privacy in the matter as all this attention can either positively or negatively affect his livelihood. The school district put out an official statement saying that it was the profanity in the song (five shits and one fuck) that was the issue, and not the song’s blistering criticism of such things as school censorship. We got word that students have organized a petition to challenge the situation. That’s wassup. Now, let’s see what happens. In the meantime, hip someone who hasn’t heard about the matter to what’s happening.

Shoutout to the good folks in Spokane keeping us posted on the matter. Shoutout to all the teachers who play ours, or any hip-hop artists, lyrics in class to spur relevant discussions in class. And shoutout to you, who cared enough to get in the conversation. As school’s just getting back in session, keep it going. We hope it all gets resolved soon and the teacher gets back in the classroom, where they belong. And if not? Well, I guess we’ll find out if that happens (but lets hope not).

“It goes one, for the…”

-Geo, Blue Scholars

item.content:encoded:
Something like this has been long overdue.

Now, thanks to affordable, bite-size technology, we are able to show you some of the story that goes on off-stage.

It also seems appropriate to share this now considering that we’re about to hit up 4 East Coast cities with our townmates, Macklemore & Ryan Lewis. If you’ve never seen us all rock together, you’re in for a treat.

Green River Community College is a modestly sized educational institution located about 45 minutes from Seattle. About 2 hours if the traffic is bad. The good folks at GRCC invited us to do a show so we took the camera along and captured a little bit of a very typical Blue Scholars day.

I was still learning how to use the camera’s basic functions when this was filmed (still trying to learn actually) so I hope you enjoy all the overexposed shots.

item.title: NEW MUSIC: Lumière (by Blue Scholars AKA us)
item.dc:creator: Sabzi
item.description: It was like November 2009 and I was rolling Beacon Ave with my friend Saman, an Iranian girl who’d grown up between the US / Kenya / England. We were in the Nissan Sentra she’d bought from a mutual friend who’d previously bought it from me, and I had bought it from another Iranian dood [...]
item.content:encoded:
It was like November 2009 and I was rolling Beacon Ave with my friend Saman, an Iranian girl who’d grown up between the US / Kenya / England. We were in the Nissan Sentra she’d bought from a mutual friend who’d previously bought it from me, and I had bought it from another Iranian dood in Whitecenter who makes some of the best homemade Joojeh Kabob you’ve ever tasted.

She was playing this record from a band called The xx she recently was referred to by a friend or something off the iPod plugged into the tape-deck thru an adapter while powered by one of those cigarette lighter things from Radio Shack.

Yea that’s right, it’s a cigarette lighter. Funny how new cars don’t have “cigarette lighters” and instead have a circular hole thing for “power supply” that you still need to buy a special adapter for. Originally, plugging your walkman, discman, and later cellphone via adapter into these lighter plugs was an innovative way of drawing power from what was available to you as a car owner.

Now smoking cigarettes is suddenly super taboo and new cars don’t have cigarette lighters built in to them, but they still have this power-hole.

My question was, if you’re gonna make a car with a power-hole, why not just make it a REGULAR OUTLET? If you’re no longer supplying the cigarette lighter, there’s no point in keeping the whole power-hole thing in it’s original form.

Well, more and more new consumer cars have regular outlets now and that makes this whole argument a little moot.

The point is, the speakers in this Nissan Sentra weren’t very good and made the the music that’s being played out of them sound all gray. For this particular record tho, that didn’t matter. Every song on this xx record was already gray (pardon me, “grey”), they all sounded the same, and they were all awesome. Perfect for a November drive in the Town.

As we listened to this record, I turned to Saman and said “you know, one of the first things Blue Scholars became known for was flipping indie-rock samples in rap songs. It fits in with our whole eclectic, international-Seattle identity. Also, the only thing that would make us even more compatible with The xx is if the only South Asian in the group, Baria Qureshi, didn’t quit the band.”

She looked back at me and said “will you please stop talking about work for 5 seconds? I DON’T CARE. Geez.”

words by Sabzi
photos by Prometheus Brown

item.title: VIDEO: Seattle 100 – Portrait of a City
item.dc:creator: Geo
item.description: Promotional video for Chase Jarvis' "Seattle 100: Portrait of a City"
item.content:encoded:
Seattle 100: Portrait of a City from 4Culture on Vimeo.

Awhile back, Chase Jarvis hit us up to be featured in his photo book Seattle 100: Portrait of a City featuring portraits and biographies of 100 Seattle creatives. And now, the book is set for release with a launch party during the upcoming City Arts Fest before it hits retail. We’re honored to be a part of this project, and it’s dope to hear one of our instrumentals as the soundtrack in the promo video (above). Check the description:

Seattle 100: Portrait of a City is the culmination of a two-year personal project by renowned photographer, filmmaker, and social artist Chase Jarvis. Seattle 100 shares more than 300 stunning blackand white portraits and biographies of each subject- a curated collection of leading artists, musicians, writers, scientists,restaurateurs, DJs, developers, activists, entrepreneurs, filmmakers, all of whom are defining and driving culture in Seattle.

Seattle based artist, Chase Jarvis, in collaboration with Small Lot Co-Op, Terra Blanca Winery, and Theo Chocolate will release a Seattle 100 book, collection of Seattle 100 wines and a Seattle 100 Theo Chocolate bar all benefitting the nonprofit, 4Culture.

A full 100 percent of proceeds from the book, wines, and chocolate bars will directly benefit 4Culture.

This book will be available at chasejarvis.com/seattle100 and at major book retail stores in the Seattle area and online.

item.title: PHOTOSET: Cougfest @ Washington State University
item.dc:creator: Geo
item.description: Photos from Washington State University Cougfest 2010.
item.content:encoded:
The five hour drive to Wazzu (I don’t care what anyone says, I’m gonna call it that for the rest of my life) is always worth it. Rival territory for Huskies like ourselves, but one thing I know is that this school parties like a mug. Makes sense, as there’s not much else to do in Pullman. We’ve seen it firsthand several times on past trips, but this time we came through for Cougfest-sans-Coolio with a whole mob of 206ers: Macklemore & Ryan Lewis, Grynch, DJ Nphared, Sol, Lace Cadence & Neema to name a few. Lots of stagediving and trees everywhere. In short, it was memorable night. So memorable that I aint even upset at leaving the extra rolls of film at the hotel before the show. In fact, it’s probably best that I did.

Now, the five hour ride back? That’s another story.
